papers.title: History and Evolution of Computers: practice set 1
papers.description: 6 original WASSCE-style objective questions on history and evolution of computers, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Who is known as the father of the computer?
questions.explanation:
Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine. The Analytical Engine had an input, a store (memory), a mill (processor) and an output, the same main parts as a modern computer, so he is called the father of the computer.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Alan Turing: Turing described the universal machine in 1936 and is often called the father of computer science.
- John von Neumann: Von Neumann set out the stored-program concept in 1945.
- Blaise Pascal: Pascal built the Pascaline, a mechanical adding machine, in 1642.

questions.stem: Which electronic component was the main part of first-generation computers?
questions.explanation:
First-generation computers (1940s–1956), such as ENIAC, used thousands of vacuum tubes (valves). They were huge, used a lot of power and gave off much heat.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- transistors: Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation.
- integrated circuits: Integrated circuits mark the third generation.
- microprocessors: Microprocessors mark the fourth generation.

questions.stem: The microprocessor is the main feature of which generation of computers?
questions.explanation:
The fourth generation (1971 to the present) is built on the microprocessor: a whole CPU on one chip, made possible by very large scale integration (VLSI). The Intel 4004 of 1971 was the first.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the first generation: The first generation used vacuum tubes.
- the second generation: The second generation used transistors.
- the third generation: The third generation used integrated circuits.

questions.stem: Who is regarded as the first computer programmer?
questions.explanation:
In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine with a step-by-step method for it to calculate a series of numbers. This is seen as the first computer program.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Charles Babbage: Babbage designed the Analytical Engine; the first program for it is credited to Lovelace.
- Herman Hollerith: Hollerith built the punched-card tabulating machine for the 1890 US census.
- John Napier: Napier invented Napier's bones, numbered rods for multiplication, in 1617.

questions.stem: Which early calculating device used beads that slide on rods?
questions.explanation:
The abacus, used thousands of years ago in Mesopotamia and China, is a frame of beads on rods used for adding and subtracting. It is the earliest known calculating aid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Napier's bones: Napier's bones were numbered rods used for multiplication.
- the slide rule: A slide rule uses sliding scales, not beads.
- the Pascaline: The Pascaline was worked by geared wheels.

questions.stem: Artificial intelligence and natural language processing are features of which generation of computers?
questions.explanation:
The fifth generation (today and the future) aims at computers that can learn, reason and understand ordinary language, using artificial intelligence and parallel processing; voice assistants and chatbots are examples.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the second generation: The second generation is marked by transistors.
- the third generation: The third generation is marked by integrated circuits.
- the first generation: The first generation used vacuum tubes and machine language.

papers.title: Classification of Computers: practice set 1
papers.description: 6 original WASSCE-style objective questions on classification of computers, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A computer that works with continuous data, such as temperature, speed or pressure, is called
questions.explanation:
Analogue computers measure continuously changing physical quantities and usually show the result on a dial or scale, as an analogue speedometer does.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a digital computer: A digital computer works with discrete data, 0s and 1s.
- a hybrid computer: A hybrid computer combines analogue and digital features.
- a microcomputer: Microcomputer is a class by size, not by the kind of data handled.

questions.stem: Which type of computer is best suited to weather forecasting?
questions.explanation:
Weather forecasting needs an enormous number of calculations done very quickly, so it is done on supercomputers, the largest and fastest computers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a minicomputer: A minicomputer serves a small organisation and is far too slow for forecasting.
- a microcomputer: A microcomputer is a personal computer for one user.
- an embedded computer: An embedded computer controls a single machine, such as a washing machine.

questions.stem: A machine in a hospital that measures a patient's heartbeat and shows it as numbers on a screen is an example of
questions.explanation:
It takes in continuous measurements (analogue) and processes and displays them as digits (digital), so it is a hybrid computer. A modern petrol pump is another example.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an analogue computer: It does more than measure: it also processes and shows the readings digitally.
- a mainframe computer: Mainframe is a size class for large organisations with many users.
- a supercomputer: A supercomputer is a very large machine for huge calculations.

questions.stem: An automated teller machine (ATM) is an example of
questions.explanation:
A special-purpose computer is designed for one particular job with a fixed program. An ATM only handles banking transactions such as giving cash and showing balances.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a general-purpose computer: A general-purpose computer can run many different programs; an ATM does one job.
- a supercomputer: An ATM is small and does simple banking transactions.
- an analogue computer: An ATM works with discrete digital data.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a microcomputer?
questions.explanation:
A microcomputer is a small computer built around one microprocessor and used by one person at a time: desktops, laptops, tablets and smartphones.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a mainframe used by a bank: A mainframe is a large computer serving thousands of users.
- a supercomputer used for climate research: A supercomputer is the largest and fastest class.
- a minicomputer serving a factory: A minicomputer is a medium-sized computer for many users.

options.label: A
options.content: a mainframe used by a bank

options.label: C
options.content: a supercomputer used for climate research

questions.stem: Digital computers represent data as
questions.explanation:
A digital computer counts rather than measures: all its data, numbers, text, pictures and sound, is held as discrete binary digits, 0 and 1.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- continuously changing physical quantities: That describes analogue computers.
- pointer positions on a dial: Dial output is typical of analogue devices.
- decimal digits stored in gears: That describes mechanical calculators such as the Pascaline.

options.label: C
options.content: discrete values made of the digits 0 and 1

papers.title: Data and Information: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on data and information, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Raw, unprocessed facts and figures are called
questions.explanation:
Data are raw facts with no meaning on their own, such as a list of marks. When processed (totalled, averaged, ranked) they become information.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- information: Information is data that has been processed and made meaningful.
- a database: A database is an organised collection of related files or tables.
- a program: A program is a set of instructions, not facts.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows the stages of the data processing cycle in the correct order?
questions.explanation:
Data is collected, entered (input), processed into information, presented (output) and saved (storage). Feedback from the output lets errors be corrected.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- input, collection, output, processing, storage: Data must be collected before it is input, and processed before it is output.
- collection, processing, input, storage, output: Data must be input before the computer can process it.
- processing, input, collection, output, storage: Processing cannot come before the data is collected and input.

questions.stem: Paying workers' salaries at the end of each month is an example of
questions.explanation:
In batch processing, transactions are collected over a period and processed together as one group. Payroll, utility bills and marking exam answer sheets are typical examples.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- real-time processing: Real-time processing handles each transaction at once, as at an ATM.
- time-sharing: Time-sharing is many users sharing one computer in turns.
- distributed processing: Distributed processing shares work among networked computers in different places.

questions.stem: Which validation check makes sure that an examination mark entered is between 0 and 100?
questions.explanation:
A range check makes sure a value lies between a lower and an upper limit; any mark below 0 or above 100 is rejected.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a presence check: A presence check only makes sure a field is not left empty.
- a length check: A length check counts the number of characters.
- a type check: A type check makes sure the data is of the right type, such as a number.

questions.stem: In the data hierarchy, a collection of related fields about one person or thing is called
questions.explanation:
The data hierarchy runs bit → byte → field → record → file → database. All the fields about one student (ID, name, class, date of birth) form one record.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a file: A file is a collection of related records.
- a field: A field is a single item of data, such as a surname.
- a byte: A byte is 8 bits, enough for one character.

questions.stem: The idea that a computer given wrong input data will give wrong output is known as
questions.explanation:
GIGO means a computer only processes what it is given: if the input data is wrong, the information produced will be wrong too, however powerful the computer is.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- verification: Verification is a check that data was copied correctly.
- feedback: Feedback is checking the output so that errors can be corrected.
- batch processing: Batch processing is a mode of processing, not a principle about errors.

questions.stem: Withdrawing cash from an ATM is an example of
questions.explanation:
In real-time processing each transaction is processed immediately, so the account balance is updated at once and the next withdrawal is checked against it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- batch processing: The withdrawal cannot wait to be processed later with other transactions.
- manual processing: The ATM processes the transaction electronically.
- mechanical processing: Mechanical processing uses machines with moving parts, such as a cash register.

papers.title: Number Systems and Data Representation: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on number systems and data representation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Convert $37_{10}$ to binary.
questions.explanation:
Divide by 2 repeatedly: $37 \div 2 = 18$ r 1, $18 \div 2 = 9$ r 0, $9 \div 2 = 4$ r 1, $4 \div 2 = 2$ r 0, $2 \div 2 = 1$ r 0, $1 \div 2 = 0$ r 1. Reading the remainders upwards gives $100101_2$. Check: $32 + 4 + 1 = 37$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 101001: This reads the remainders downwards; it is 41, not 37.
- 100111: This is 39: the 2s place should be 0.
- 110101: This is 53: the 16s place should be 0.

questions.stem: Convert $110010_2$ to decimal.
questions.explanation:
Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The 1s are in the 32, 16 and 2 places, so $32 + 16 + 2 = 50$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 19: This reads the bits in reverse order (010011).
- 52: This uses 4 instead of 2 for the second bit from the right.
- 48: This leaves out the 2s place.

questions.stem: Convert $3F_{16}$ to decimal.
questions.explanation:
F = 15. The places are 16s and units, so $3F_{16} = 3 \times 16 + 15 = 48 + 15 = 63$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 45: This multiplies 3 by 10 instead of 16.
- 18: This simply adds 3 and 15.
- 315: This writes 3 and 15 side by side.

questions.stem: Add the binary numbers $1011_2 + 101_2$.
questions.explanation:
From the right: $1 + 1 = 10$, write 0 carry 1; $1 + 0 + 1 = 10$, write 0 carry 1; $0 + 1 + 1 = 10$, write 0 carry 1; $1 + 0 + 1 = 10$, write 0 carry 1; the last carry gives 1. Answer: $10000_2$. Check: $11 + 5 = 16$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1111: This ignores the carries: 1 + 1 = 10 in binary, so write 0 and carry 1.
- 10001: This is 17; the sum of 11 and 5 is 16.
- 1110: This is 14; a carry has been lost.

questions.stem: How many bits make one byte?
questions.explanation:
A byte is a group of 8 bits, enough to store one character such as a letter or a digit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4: 4 bits make a nibble, half a byte.
- 16: 16 bits make two bytes.
- 1024: 1024 is the number of bytes in a kilobyte.

questions.stem: In the ASCII code, the capital letter A is represented by the decimal number
questions.explanation:
In ASCII, A = 65, B = 66 and so on; small a = 97; the digit 0 = 48. 65 in binary is 1000001, which fits in the 7 bits of standard ASCII.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 97: 97 is the code for small a.
- 48: 48 is the code for the digit 0.
- 1: ASCII codes for letters do not start at 1.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a valid octal number?
questions.explanation:
The octal (base-8) system uses only the digits 0 to 7. The number 278 contains the digit 8, so it cannot be an octal number.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 157: 157 uses only the digits 0 to 7, so it is a valid octal number.
- 720: 720 uses only the digits 0 to 7, so it is a valid octal number.
- 1046: 1046 uses only the digits 0 to 7, so it is a valid octal number.

papers.title: The CPU: practice set 1
papers.description: 6 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the cpu, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which part of the CPU performs calculations and comparisons?
questions.explanation:
The ALU carries out arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logic operations (comparisons and AND, OR, NOT) that let programs make decisions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the control unit: The control unit fetches, decodes and directs; it does not calculate.
- the program counter: The program counter is a register that holds the next instruction's address.
- the data bus: The data bus carries data between parts; it does no processing.

questions.stem: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.explanation:
The program counter holds the address of the next instruction. During the fetch stage its value is copied to the MAR and it then goes up by one.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the accumulator: The accumulator holds the result of the latest ALU calculation.
- the memory data register (MDR): The MDR holds the data or instruction being moved to or from memory.
- the current instruction register (CIR): The CIR holds the instruction being decoded and carried out now.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct order of the stages of the machine cycle?
questions.explanation:
For every instruction the CPU fetches it from memory, decodes it in the control unit, then executes it, often using the ALU. The cycle repeats billions of times a second.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- decode, fetch, execute: An instruction must be fetched before it can be decoded.
- execute, fetch, decode: An instruction cannot be carried out before it is fetched and decoded.
- fetch, execute, decode: The CPU must decode an instruction before it can carry it out.

questions.stem: Which bus carries the address of a memory location from the CPU to memory?
questions.explanation:
The address bus carries addresses one way, from the CPU, to say which memory location or device is to be used. The data then travels on the data bus.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the data bus: The data bus carries the data itself, in both directions.
- the control bus: The control bus carries signals such as read, write and clock timing.
- a USB cable: A USB cable connects external devices; it is not one of the CPU's internal buses.

questions.stem: The clock speed of a processor is measured in
questions.explanation:
Clock speed is the number of cycles a second, measured in hertz; a 3 GHz processor completes 3 billion cycles a second.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gigabytes (GB): Gigabytes measure memory and storage capacity.
- dots per inch (dpi): Dots per inch measure print or scan quality.
- pages per minute (ppm): Pages per minute measure printer speed.

questions.stem: Which part of the CPU directs and coordinates the operations of all the other parts of the computer?
questions.explanation:
The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals that direct the ALU, memory and input and output devices, keeping all operations in step.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the arithmetic and logic unit: The ALU does calculations and comparisons under the control unit's direction.
- the accumulator: The accumulator is a register that stores results.
- cache memory: Cache memory stores frequently used data; it gives no commands.

papers.title: Input Devices: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on input devices, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which input device is used to mark the objective answer sheets of an examination?
questions.explanation:
An optical mark reader detects marks made in fixed places on a form, so it can tell which box in each row has been shaded.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an optical character reader (OCR): OCR recognises letters and digits; it does not detect shaded boxes.
- a magnetic ink character reader (MICR): MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques.
- a barcode reader: A barcode reader reads bars printed on products.

questions.stem: Magnetic ink character recognition (MICR) is mainly used to
questions.explanation:
Banks print the cheque number, bank code and account number in magnetic ink. MICR reads them quickly and accurately, and the characters are hard to forge.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- read prices on goods in a supermarket: Supermarkets use barcode readers.
- mark multiple-choice answer sheets: Answer sheets are marked by OMR.
- identify people by their fingerprints: Fingerprints are read by biometric scanners.

options.label: A
options.content: read prices on goods in a supermarket

options.label: B
options.content: read the numbers printed on bank cheques

questions.stem: Which key deletes the character to the left of the cursor?
questions.explanation:
Backspace moves the cursor back one place and deletes the character to its left; Delete removes the character to the right of the cursor or a selected item.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Delete: Delete removes the character to the right of the cursor.
- Esc: Esc cancels the current action or closes a menu.
- Tab: Tab moves the cursor to the next tab stop.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pointing device?
questions.explanation:
Pointing devices move a pointer on the screen and select items: the mouse, touchpad, trackball, joystick, light pen, stylus and touch screen.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a scanner: A scanner copies documents as images; it does not move a pointer.
- a microphone: A microphone inputs sound.
- a barcode reader: A barcode reader reads codes on products.

questions.stem: A fingerprint scanner used to record staff attendance is an example of
questions.explanation:
Biometric devices identify a person by a body feature such as a fingerprint, the face, the iris or the voice.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a pointing device: A pointing device moves a pointer on the screen.
- an output device: The scanner takes in data; it does not present results.
- a storage device: A storage device keeps data; the scanner inputs it.

questions.stem: Which input device does a supermarket use at its tills to identify goods quickly?
questions.explanation:
A barcode reader reads the pattern of bars printed on each product, so the till finds the item and its price instantly and without typing errors.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an optical mark reader: OMR reads shaded marks on forms.
- a light pen: A light pen draws or selects on a screen.
- a MICR reader: MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques.

questions.stem: Which technology turns a scanned page of printed text into text that can be edited?
questions.explanation:
OCR software recognises the letters and digits in an image of a page and turns them into editable text, for example in a word processor.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- optical mark recognition (OMR): OMR detects marks in fixed places; it does not recognise letters.
- magnetic ink character recognition (MICR): MICR reads only characters printed in magnetic ink.
- speech recognition: Speech recognition turns spoken words, not printed text, into text.

papers.title: Output Devices: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on output devices, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an impact printer?
questions.explanation:
Impact printers form characters by striking an inked ribbon against the paper. The dot-matrix printer's pins strike the ribbon, so it is an impact printer, like daisy-wheel and line printers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a laser printer: A laser printer fuses toner onto the paper without striking it.
- an inkjet printer: An inkjet printer sprays ink; nothing strikes the paper.
- a thermal printer: A thermal printer uses heat on special paper.

questions.stem: Output printed on paper is called
questions.explanation:
Hard copy is permanent output on paper or another material that can be read without a computer; soft copy is temporary output on a screen or as sound.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- soft copy: Soft copy is output shown on a screen or heard through a speaker.
- a pixel: A pixel is the smallest dot of light on a screen.
- a backup: A backup is a spare copy of files kept for safety.

questions.stem: Which output device is best for producing large building plans and engineering drawings?
questions.explanation:
A plotter draws high-quality, large-size drawings such as plans, maps and engineering designs, using pens or ink jets.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a dot-matrix printer: A dot-matrix printer gives low-quality output on ordinary paper sizes.
- a projector: A projector gives soft copy on a screen, not a printed plan.
- a thermal printer: A thermal printer prints small receipts and tickets.

questions.stem: The smallest dot of light that makes up a picture on a screen is called
questions.explanation:
Pixel is short for picture element. Every image on a screen is made of pixels; the more pixels (the higher the resolution), the sharper the picture.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a bit: A bit is a binary digit, 0 or 1.
- a byte: A byte is a group of 8 bits.
- a resolution: Resolution is the number of pixels a screen shows, such as 1920 × 1080.

questions.stem: Which of the following is both an input device and an output device?
questions.explanation:
A touch screen shows output like a monitor and also takes input when you touch it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a scanner: A scanner is an input device only.
- a printer: A printer is an output device only.
- a keyboard: A keyboard is an input device only.

questions.stem: Till receipts in a supermarket are usually printed by
questions.explanation:
A thermal printer uses heat on heat-sensitive paper. It is small, quiet and needs no ink, so it is used for receipts, ATM slips and tickets.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a plotter: A plotter draws large plans and maps.
- a daisy-wheel printer: Daisy-wheel printers are old, slow letter-quality printers.
- a 3D printer: A 3D printer builds solid objects, not receipts.

questions.stem: The quality of a printer's output is measured in
questions.explanation:
Print quality (resolution) is measured in dots per inch: the more dots in each inch, the finer the print. Speed is measured in pages per minute or characters per second.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pages per minute (ppm): Pages per minute measure printing speed, not quality.
- gigahertz (GHz): Gigahertz measure a processor's clock speed.
- megabytes (MB): Megabytes measure data and storage capacity.

papers.title: Memory and Storage Devices: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on memory and storage devices, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
questions.explanation:
RAM (random access memory) is volatile: it holds the programs and data in use and loses them when the power goes off. That is why work must be saved to storage.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ROM: ROM is non-volatile; it keeps its contents without power.
- a hard disk: A hard disk is non-volatile secondary storage.
- a flash drive: Flash memory is non-volatile.

questions.stem: Which type of ROM can be erased with ultraviolet light and programmed again?
questions.explanation:
EPROM (erasable programmable ROM) is erased by shining ultraviolet light through a window on the chip, then rewritten. EEPROM is erased electrically; flash memory is a kind of EEPROM.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- PROM: A PROM can be written only once.
- EEPROM: EEPROM is erased electrically, not with ultraviolet light.
- DRAM: DRAM is a type of RAM, not ROM.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an optical storage medium?
questions.explanation:
Optical discs, CD, DVD and Blu-ray, are written and read with a laser. Hard disks and tape are magnetic; flash drives and SSDs are solid-state.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a hard disk: A hard disk is magnetic storage.
- a USB flash drive: A flash drive is solid-state storage.
- magnetic tape: Magnetic tape is magnetic storage.

questions.stem: The usual storage capacity of a standard CD is about
questions.explanation:
A CD holds about 700 MB, a single-layer DVD 4.7 GB and a single-layer Blu-ray disc 25 GB.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.7 GB: 4.7 GB is the capacity of a single-layer DVD.
- 25 GB: 25 GB is the capacity of a single-layer Blu-ray disc.
- 1.44 MB: 1.44 MB was the capacity of a floppy disk.

questions.stem: A small amount of very fast memory between the CPU and main memory, holding the most frequently used data, is called
questions.explanation:
Cache memory, usually SRAM, sits on or near the CPU and keeps copies of the data and instructions used most often, so the CPU does not wait for slower RAM.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- virtual memory: Virtual memory is part of the disk used as extra RAM, which is slower, not faster.
- ROM: ROM holds fixed start-up instructions.
- secondary storage: Secondary storage is much slower than main memory.

questions.stem: Which of the following storage devices has no moving parts?
questions.explanation:
An SSD stores data in flash memory chips with no moving parts, so it is faster, silent and less easily damaged by knocks than a hard disk.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a hard disk drive: A hard disk has spinning platters and moving read/write heads.
- a DVD drive: A DVD drive spins the disc under a laser.
- a magnetic tape drive: A tape drive winds the tape past the heads.

questions.stem: The start-up instructions (BIOS) of a computer are kept in
questions.explanation:
ROM is non-volatile, so the start-up instructions are still there when the computer is switched on and can load the operating system from storage.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- RAM: RAM is volatile, so the instructions would be lost each time the computer is switched off.
- cache memory: Cache holds copies of frequently used data while the computer runs.
- the accumulator: The accumulator is a CPU register that holds a calculation result.
